title: COP31: Future of fossil fuels exposes sharp divides among countries, yet again
syllabus: GS3 › Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation; climate change and international negotiations · GS2 › Important international institutions (UNFCCC); agreements affecting India's interests · GS4 › Environmental ethics
summary: COP31's latest draft text in Antalya dropped every mention of fossil fuels, softened the 1.5°C language and left out a US$120 billion adaptation finance target, a day before the talks were due to end.
evolution: COP28, Dubai: 'fossil fuels' named in the main agreement for the first time.
COP30, Brazil: fossil fuels left out of the final decision despite 80+ countries pressing.
India not committed to the '35 by 35' electrification target (COP31 preview card).
COP31 opens in Antalya as the 'Implementation COP'; WMO says 2026 among the warmest years.
Latest draft drops all fossil fuel references and the adaptation finance target.
ideas: Fossil fuels erased again: the first draft called for 'accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels'; the latest drops every mention, repeating Brazil (COP30).
GS3 · Climate negotiations
Dropping fossil fuels from COP texts shows that the core cause of warming remains the hardest issue to negotiate.
Three camps: the EU and over 80 countries want a phase-out roadmap; oil producers oppose it; major consumers such as India and China are not enthusiastic.
GS2 · International negotiations / GS3 · Energy security
Climate talks divide producers, consumers and ambitious blocs, so consensus language on fossil fuels stays weak.
1.5°C quietly slipping: the new text only pursues efforts toward 1.5°C and limits the overshoot, after a 1.7–1.8°C rise was judged inevitable; the 1.5°C work programme was dropped.
GS3 · Climate change
The shift from 'return to 1.5°C' to 'limit the overshoot' marks a quiet retreat from the Paris goal.
Developing countries lose on finance: the US$120 billion adaptation finance target was dropped from the draft.
GS3 · Climate finance / GS2 · Global South
Without finance targets, an 'Implementation COP' risks leaving developing countries to adapt on their own.
Electrification enters the text: the host Türkiye's push to raise electricity's share of final energy from 23% to 35% moved from a voluntary pledge into the negotiated decision.
GS3 · Energy transition
Electrification targets, though easier to agree than phase-outs, raise questions of finance and national circumstances for India.
keywords: Temporarily exceeding 1.5°C before trying to bring temperatures back down
COP31's draft accepts an overshoot and only seeks to limit its duration and magnitude.
Phrase from COP28 for moving energy systems off coal, oil and gas
The COP28 call to transition away from fossil fuels has proved hard to repeat in later COP texts.
A timeline for ending fossil fuel use, pushed by the EU
At least eight European countries have their own phase-out roadmaps, but no global one exists.
UNFCCC principle that rich and poor countries owe different efforts
India's caution on phase-out targets rests on common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.
Outcomes diluted so every party can agree
Consensus-based COPs often produce lowest-common-denominator texts on contested issues like fossil fuels.
data: Electricity's share of global final energy consumption: present level and proposed target
COP31's draft calls for raising electricity's share of global final energy use from 23% to 35%.
Proposed adaptation finance target dropped from the COP31 draft
A proposed US$120 billion adaptation finance target was dropped from the COP31 draft.
examples: first COP text to name fossil fuels
COP28 Dubai, 2023: first COP decision to name fossil fuels.
GS3 · Climate negotiations · GS4 · Environmental ethics
COP31 Antalya draft, 2026: every mention of fossil fuels erased.
'35 by 35': Türkiye's push to raise electricity's share of final energy.
pyqs: India's Paris commitments, COP26 and the updated NDC.
Major outcomes of COP26 and India's commitments.
India's changing climate policy in international fora.
50% renewables by 2030; shifting subsidies from fossil fuels.
Global warming and control measures under the Kyoto Protocol.
Carbon credits and CDM under the UNFCCC.
Global warming as an outcome of human greed in the name of development.

trend.t: Climate negotiation questions began with UNFCCC mechanisms (carbon credits 2014, Kyoto 2022), moved to specific COP outcomes and India's pledges (COP26 in 2021, Paris and NDCs in 2025), and to India's evolving stance in global fora (2022). The energy-transition side appears through renewables targets and fossil fuel subsidies (2022) and, in GS4, through greed and development (2024).
trend.watch: UPSC asked India's COP commitments in 2021 and again in 2025, each time pairing a specific COP outcome with India's pledges, so COP outcomes and India's position on fossil fuel transition are a must-study.
focus: India's position on fossil fuel phase-out vs phase-down
Climate finance and adaptation for developing countries
1.5°C goal, overshoot and the Paris Agreement
Energy transition: electrification, renewables and subsidies

potential: "The phase-out of fossil fuels remains the most divisive issue in climate negotiations." Discuss in the context of recent COP meetings and India's position. (15 marks)
Why has climate finance for adaptation remained elusive for developing countries? Suggest measures. (10 marks)
"Keeping the 1.5°C goal alive now means managing an overshoot." Examine. (10 marks)

practice.q: "The phase-out of fossil fuels remains the most divisive issue in climate negotiations." Discuss in the context of recent COP meetings and India's position.

answer.t: Named in a COP decision for the first time only at COP28 (2023), fossil fuels were dropped again from COP30's final text and from COP31's latest draft in Antalya (November 2026).

pts.t: Oil and gas exporters depend on fossil revenue and resist any phase-out timeline.
pts.ex: Major oil producers oppose an EU-led roadmap at COP31.

pts.t: Growing economies still rely on coal and oil for affordable energy.
pts.ex: India and China 'not too enthusiastic' about phase-out.

pts.t: Developing countries argue the rich, who emitted most, must cut first and pay.
Transition costs are high, and promised finance has fallen short.
pts.ex: US$120 billion adaptation finance target dropped at COP31.

pts.t: Any party can block, so texts shrink to agreed minimums.
pts.ex: Over 80 countries pressed at COP30, yet fossil fuels were left out.

pts.t: Wars and supply shocks make countries cling to secure fuels.
pts.ex: Disruptions to global energy supply highlighted by India.

pts.t: India prefers gradual, nationally determined transition.
India pairs caution on targets with rapid renewable growth.
pts.ex: Net zero by 2070; 50% non-fossil power capacity target.

pts.t: India resists global targets that ignore development needs.
pts.ex: Not committed to the '35 by 35' electrification target.

pts.t: India demands finance and technology from developed countries.
pts.ex: India's support for the Loss and Damage Fund.

pts.t: Without curbing fossil fuels, 1.5°C becomes unreachable.
Repeated dilution erodes trust in multilateral climate action.
Countries act alone, creating uneven standards.
pts.ex: Eight European countries with their own roadmaps.

pts.t: Poor and island nations face rising losses.
pts.ex: Nepal's Loss and Damage payout covering a fraction of need.

pts.t: Rich nations phase out first; developing nations follow with support.
Firm adaptation and transition finance targets.
Protect coal-dependent workers and regions.
Agree on achievable steps such as electrification and efficiency.
pts.ex: Electricity share from 23% to 35% in the draft.

pts.t: Cheaper access to storage, green hydrogen and CCUS.
pts.ex: International Solar Alliance as a model.

pts.t: Shift fossil fuel subsidies to renewables.

answer.t: From Dubai to Antalya, fossil fuels remain the elephant in the room; only a transition that is fair, financed and differentiated can bring every country to the table.

title: Why fixing India's air pollution crisis requires more than technical solutions
where: Explained page, 'Expert Explains' (Shahzad Gani, Centre for Atmospheric Sciences, IIT Delhi)
syllabus: GS3 › Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation · GS2 › Government policies and interventions; vulnerable sections · GS4 › Environmental ethics; probity in use of public funds
summary: An IIT Delhi atmospheric scientist argues that India knows the sources of its air pollution and must act on them through transport, clean cooking, waste management and regulation, rather than wait for more data or chase technological spectacles.
evolution: Punjab farm fires concentrated in Tarn Taran and Amritsar.
Clean air needs targets, timelines, accountability; NCAP 2.0 being drafted.
Acting before the air turns severe.
Expert view: sources known, act now; look beyond technical fixes.
ideas: A year-round, all-India problem: air pollution is not just Delhi-NCR in winter; transport, household fuels, waste burning, industry and construction pollute all year, while weather only disperses or traps emissions.
GS3 · Pollution
Treating air pollution as a seasonal Delhi issue misses its year-round, nationwide sources.

Sources are known, so act: reducing pollution needs two things, fewer emission sources and cleaner remaining ones; public transport, clean cooking and heating, alternatives to stubble burning, working waste management and industrial regulation.
GS3 · Pollution control / GS2 · Policy
Research should refine interventions, not become a prerequisite for action.
Beyond technical fixes: stubble burning needs an understanding of farmers' economic constraints; firecracker pollution needs changes in social attitudes and community action, not only bans.
GS3 · Agriculture / GS1 · Society
Stubble and firecrackers are social and economic problems, not merely technical ones.

Measure what people breathe: rooftop monitors miss indoor exposure from solid-fuel cooking, which falls mostly on women; street vendors, construction and sanitation workers, and farmers face the highest exposure.
GS2 · Vulnerable sections / GS1 · Women
Exposure, not ambient readings alone, should guide policy so that the most vulnerable are protected.

Spectacle vs substance: smog towers and artificial rain offer the optics of action despite doubts over effectiveness; institutional fixes such as transport, waste and clean energy need sustained funding, coordination and confronting vested interests.
GS3 · Governance of environment / GS4 · Probity
Public money should fund what cuts emissions, not what looks like action.
keywords: Judging success by what people actually breathe, indoors and outdoors
An exposure-centred clean air policy would cover kitchens and workplaces, not just rooftop monitors.
Belief that a gadget can fix a complex social problem
Smog towers reflect techno-solutionism: visible, costly and of doubtful effect.
Visible measures that signal effort without reducing harm
Spectacular projects can give governments the optics of action without cutting emissions.
Fair sharing of environmental burdens and protection
Those with the least choice, such as street vendors and women cooking on solid fuels, bear the most exposure: an environmental justice gap.
Valuing economists, social scientists and practitioners alongside scientists
Clean air needs plural expertise, from agricultural economists to community workers.
examples: spectacle over substance in pollution control
Smog towers and artificial rain: the optics of action without real emission cuts.
A rooftop monitor cannot see a smoky kitchen: indoor exposure falls mostly on women.
GS2 · Vulnerable sections · GS4 · Environmental justice
Street vendors and sanitation workers: highest exposure, least choice.
pyqs: Key features of the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP).
WHO's revised Air Quality Guidelines and changes needed in NCAP.
Photochemical smog: formation, effects, mitigation; Gothenburg Protocol.
Why air pollution is worse in Delhi than in Mumbai and Kolkata.
Challenges to solid waste management; policy framework.
National Urban Transport Policy: 'moving people' not 'moving vehicles'.

trend.t: Air pollution questions began with geography (why Delhi is worse, 2015), moved to policy (NCAP features 2020, WHO guidelines and NCAP changes 2021) and science (photochemical smog 2022). Related sources are asked separately: urban transport (2014) and solid waste management (2026).
trend.watch: Air quality was asked three years in a row (2020, 2021, 2022), each time linking science or standards to NCAP, so NCAP and its revision (NCAP 2.0) are must-study, along with source-sectors such as transport and waste.
focus: Sector-wise sources: transport, household fuels, waste, stubble

potential: "India's air pollution crisis is less a problem of knowledge than of implementation." Discuss. (15 marks)
Why have technological fixes such as smog towers failed to address air pollution? Suggest a more effective approach. (10 marks)
Examine how air pollution affects vulnerable sections disproportionately. (10 marks)

practice.q: "India's air pollution crisis is less a problem of knowledge than of implementation." Discuss.
parts: Why it is a problem of implementation

answer.t: The sources of India's air pollution, from transport and household fuels to waste and stubble burning, are well established, yet unhealthy air persists across the country all year round.

answer.h: Why it is a problem of implementation

pts.t: Sources are mapped, but cleaner transport, fuels and waste systems lag.
pts.ex: Year-round emissions from transport, waste burning and construction.

pts.t: Funds flow to visible gadgets of doubtful effect.
Pollution control boards are short of staff and powers.
pts.ex: Patchy enforcement on industry and construction dust.

pts.t: Airsheds cross state boundaries, but action is state-bound.
pts.ex: Stubble burning in Punjab, smog in Delhi.

pts.t: Rankings reward spending and plans, not cleaner air.
Reform hits powerful lobbies in transport, industry and energy.
Ambient monitors miss what people breathe indoors and at work.
Monitoring is thin outside metros.
pts.ex: Air pollution is all-India, not only Delhi-NCR.

pts.t: Farmers' and households' choices are under-studied.
Secondary pollutant formation remains uncertain.
Public transport, clean cooking, waste management and industrial regulation.
pts.ex: 'Moving people, not vehicles' (National Urban Transport Policy).

pts.t: Measure success by reduced exposure, with deadlines and accountability.
Regional bodies with powers across states.
pts.ex: Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR.

pts.t: Make alternatives to burning economically viable.
Safer workplaces and clean fuels for the poorest.
pts.ex: Clean cooking access for poor households.

pts.t: Independent evaluation of costly interventions.
pts.ex: Civil society questioning smog tower spending.

answer.t: India does not need to know everything to act on what it already knows; clean air depends on institutions, not gadgets.

title: Silence on the cause: fossil fuels dropped from COP31's draft
news: COP31's latest draft removed every mention of fossil fuels, the main source of greenhouse gas emissions, along with an adaptation finance target for developing countries.
syllabus: Environmental ethics; intergenerational equity; climate justice
link: Avoiding the main cause of warming to protect present interests shifts the cost onto future generations and the most vulnerable countries. Honesty about causes and fairness in sharing burdens are the ethical tests of climate diplomacy.
question: "Climate negotiations that avoid naming the cause of the problem fail both future generations and the vulnerable." Discuss the ethical issues involved.

title: Clean air for whom? Optics, spending and the most exposed
news: An IIT Delhi scientist says smog towers and artificial rain give governments the optics of action, while street vendors, sanitation workers and women cooking on solid fuels bear the highest exposure.
syllabus: Environmental ethics; probity in use of public funds; concern for the vulnerable
link: Spending public money on visible but ineffective fixes is a failure of probity and stewardship. Fair policy puts those with the least choice and the most exposure first.
question: "Public spending on environmental problems must be judged by outcomes, not optics." Discuss with reference to air pollution control.

title: 'Implementation COP' must live up to its name
syllabus: GS3 › Conservation, environmental pollution and degradation; climate change · GS2 › Important international institutions, agencies and fora (UNFCCC) · GS3 › Disaster management (adaptation, early warning)
summary: As COP31 opens in Antalya, Türkiye, the editorial says it must narrow the gap between commitments and delivery: finance for clean energy in developing countries, adaptation and a funded Loss and Damage Fund.
evolution: Editorial and op-eds on looking beyond old climate fault lines ahead of COP31 (climate thread).
COP31 opens in Antalya, Türkiye, billed as the 'Implementation COP'.
ideas: From pledges to delivery: 1.5°C overshoot now near-certain.
GS3 · Climate / GS2 · UNFCCC
The gap is implementation, not ambition.
Developing economies (ex-China) got 18% of clean-energy investment in 2025.
GS3 · Climate finance
The transition is unequal by finance.
High cost of capital, not technology, blocks Southern clean energy.
GS3 · Climate finance
Lower the cost of money, not just of panels.
Adaptation and a funded Loss and Damage Fund are now urgent.
GS3 · Adaptation / GS4 · Climate justice
Those who emitted least pay most.
keywords: The distance between climate commitments and actual delivery
COP31's test is the implementation gap, not another round of pledges.
The interest and risk premium that makes projects costlier in poorer countries
A solar plant costs more in Africa than in Europe because of the cost of capital, not sunlight.
Moving to clean energy fairly, without leaving workers or poorer nations behind
India's case at COPs rests on a just transition backed by finance and technology.
Warming temporarily exceeding 1.5°C before any return
Near-certain overshoot of 1.5°C makes adaptation as urgent as mitigation.
data: Share of global clean-energy investment received in 2025 by emerging and developing economies outside China (nearly two-thirds of world population)
Developing economies outside China, home to two-thirds of humanity, got only 18% of clean-energy investment in 2025.
People in Africa still without electricity
Nearly 600 million Africans still lack electricity despite the continent's vast renewable potential.
examples: GS3 · Loss and damage · GS4 · Climate justice
Nepal floods: least emitters, highest costs.
huge solar potential, 600 million without power
Africa: huge solar potential, 600 million without power.
International Solar Alliance: South–South climate cooperation.
pyqs: India's climate policy in international fora.
Global warming as outcome of human greed in the name of development.

trend.t: Climate questions moved from treaty history (Kyoto, 2022) to COP outcomes and India's commitments (COP26 in 2021; NDC update in 2025) and India's diplomatic stance (2022). Adaptation enters through disaster resilience and Sendai targets (2024).
trend.watch: A COP-and-commitments question was asked in 2021 and 2025, so COP30–COP31 outcomes on finance, adaptation and loss and damage are likely material for the next one.
focus: Climate finance and the cost of capital
Adaptation and the Loss and Damage Fund
Climate justice as an ethics theme

potential: "The climate crisis is now a crisis of delivery, not of ambition." Examine in the context of COP31. (15 marks)
Why does clean energy remain costlier in developing countries? Suggest measures to close the climate finance gap. (10 marks)
Discuss the significance of the Loss and Damage Fund for countries like India and its neighbours. (10 marks)

practice.q: "The climate crisis is now a crisis of delivery, not of ambition." Examine in the context of COP31.

answer.t: COP31 opens in Antalya billed as the 'Implementation COP', a year after COP30 in Belém, with the world close to overshooting the 1.5°C limit set at Paris.

pts.k: Finance does not reach the South
pts.t: Clean-energy money is concentrated in rich economies and China.
pts.ex: Developing economies outside China got 18% of clean-energy investment in 2025.

pts.t: Renewable projects in developing countries cost several times more to finance.
pts.ex: High borrowing costs and public debt limit investment.

pts.t: Solar, EVs and storage are cheaper but adoption is uneven.
pts.ex: Africa's vast potential yet 600 million without electricity.

pts.t: Early warning and resilient infrastructure lag behind rising disasters.
pts.ex: Floods, heat waves and droughts more frequent since Belém.

pts.t: The fund lacks predictable and sufficient money.
pts.ex: Nepal floods: least emitters, steepest costs.

pts.t: Targets raised without removing barriers to deployment.
pts.ex: The editorial's call to address barriers 'rather than simply urging' higher targets.

pts.t: Existing commitments are inadequate.
Belém's transition outcome needs timelines.
pts.ex: Transition away from fossil fuels agreed at COP30.

pts.t: Extreme weather may intensify, raising stakes.
pts.ex: Threat of a super El Niño.

pts.t: Guarantees, blended finance and MDB reform for clean energy.
pts.ex: Risk-sharing for solar in Africa and South Asia.

pts.t: Differentiated pace with support for countries like India.
Early-warning systems and resilient infrastructure for vulnerable communities.
Predictable contributions to the Loss and Damage Fund.
pts.ex: Support for Himalayan countries like Nepal.

pts.t: Track finance delivered, not just pledged.
Share technology and finance models.

answer.t: COP31 will be judged not by new numbers but by whether a solar panel, a flood warning and a rebuilding fund actually reach those who need them.

title: Environmental groups embrace AI, even as they warn of data centre impacts
syllabus: GS3 › Conservation; biodiversity · GS3 › Science and technology in everyday life · GS3 › Climate change · GS4 › Environmental ethics
summary: Conservation groups use AI to track forest fires and count wildlife but worry about the electricity and water used by data centres; the trade-offs are expected to feature at COP31.
ideas: AI counts wildlife and flags fires in hours, not months.
GS3 · Biodiversity
Measurable nature becomes investable nature.
Data centres: ~945 TWh electricity by 2030 (IEA).
GS3 · Climate / water
AI for the planet has a planetary bill.
keywords: Developing and deploying AI within environmental limits
Sustainable AI asks not only what AI can do for nature, but what it costs nature.
Measuring ecosystems well enough to attract finance
AI-based counts can make nature investable by proving conservation outcomes.
data: Projected annual electricity use of global data centres, equal to over 300 million tonnes of CO2
The IEA projects data centres will use about 945 TWh of electricity a year by 2030.
Data-centre water use may double to 1.2 trillion litres by 2030, the IEA estimates.
examples: Kenya's AI wildlife census: 200,000 images analysed in hours.
pyqs: AI, drones, GIS and remote sensing in planning.

trend.t: Technology-for-environment questions grew from remote sensing and GIS in planning (2025) to satellites for climate-smart agriculture (2026); biodiversity came through the Kunming–Montreal framework (2026).
trend.watch: Technology applied to environment was asked in 2025 and 2026, so AI's role in conservation, and its own footprint, is worth preparing.
focus: AI and remote sensing for conservation
Energy and water footprint of data centres

potential: Discuss the potential and the environmental costs of artificial intelligence in biodiversity conservation. (10 marks)

title: The mud kitchen in Kangra breathes with the seasons
syllabus: GS1 › Indian heritage (vernacular architecture) · GS3 › Disaster management (landslides, earthquakes) · GS3 › Environment · GS2 › Government policies (PMAY, building codes) · Essay
summary: Concrete homes in Himachal trap heat and damp and load fragile slopes, while traditional mud, stone and timber houses suit the climate and quakes; codes, PMAY rules and banks still favour cement.
ideas: Mud, stone and slate homes suit climate; concrete traps heat and damp.
GS1 · Vernacular architecture
Tradition as climate adaptation.
Kath-kuni and dhajji-dewari resist quakes; concrete loads slopes.
GS3 · Disaster management
What bends survives.
Codes, PMAY and banks favour cement; recognise traditional homes as pucca.
GS2 · Housing policy
Align schemes with resilience.
keywords: The development load an area can bear without degradation
Himachal's slopes were built on without carrying-capacity studies, and the 2023 landslides followed.
Local building traditions shaped by climate and materials
Vernacular architecture is climate adaptation that predates the climate crisis.
Himachali technique of interlocking deodar timber and dry stone
Kath-kuni walls flex in earthquakes, while concrete cracks.
The Supreme Court's 2025 principle while rejecting a hotel on Shimla's forested slopes
The SC's 'ecology must come before revenue' sets the test for hill development.
data: Growth in registered hotels and homestays in Himachal, 2016–2025
Central Empowered Committee (cited by the author)
Himachal's homestays grew 670% in a decade, much of it concrete on unstable slopes.
examples: 2023 Himachal landslides: blocked drainage and heavy buildings (GSI).
lost dignity of labour, lost skills
GS1 · Society · GS4 · Dignity of labour
'Mudwork is dirty': lost dignity of labour, lost skills.
pyqs: Fast infrastructure vs disaster-risk reduction in fragile areas.

trend.t: Disaster questions shifted from describing hazards (landslides 2021, cloudbursts 2022, 2024) to governance: resilience and Sendai targets (2024), and in 2026 both fast infrastructure versus risk reduction in fragile areas and community participation.
trend.watch: Two 2026 questions asked about development in fragile areas and community roles, so Himalayan construction, building codes and traditional knowledge are high-value material.

potential: "Traditional knowledge can be a strong ally in disaster risk reduction in the Himalayas." Discuss with examples. (15 marks)
How do building norms and housing schemes shape disaster vulnerability in hill states? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Traditional knowledge can be a strong ally in disaster risk reduction in the Himalayas." Discuss with examples.

answer.t: After the 2023 monsoon disasters, the Geological Survey of India linked landslides in Kullu, Mandi and Shimla to blocked drainage, heavy multi-storey buildings and 90-degree hill cuts, not just to rain.

pts.t: Interlocking timber and dry stone flex instead of cracking.
pts.ex: Kath-kuni in Kullu and Shimla; dhajji-dewari in Kangra and Chamba.

pts.t: Stone foundations let rainwater drain; concrete blocks it and loads slopes.
pts.ex: GSI findings on blocked drainage in 2023.

pts.t: Mud walls keep homes cool in summer and warm in winter, reducing energy use.
Lighter structures suit fragile slopes.
Settlements traditionally avoided unstable slopes and streams.
Traditional masons maintain safe practices.
Building codes, PWD price lists and bylaws obstruct mud-and-stone plans.
pts.ex: National Building Code and fire bylaws.

pts.t: PMAY favours brick and cement; banks deny loans and insurance for mud homes.
Forest laws trapped villagers' bartandari timber rights in red tape.
pts.ex: 1980 Forest Conservation Act and 1996 felling limits.

pts.t: Mudwork seen as 'dirty' and concrete as modern.
Few artisans and costly natural-building architects.
Tourism boom drives quick concrete construction.
Recognise engineered mud, kath-kuni and dhajji-dewari as pucca and insurable.
Make traditional designs eligible under PMAY and for bank loans.
ITIs to teach earth building; pay master masons to train.
Mandatory studies before multi-storey construction on slopes.
Apply the Supreme Court's principle to hill projects.
Use local knowledge in village disaster plans.

answer.t: When monsoon clouds burst or fault lines shift, what bends survives: Himalayan resilience may lie less in a cement bag than in the wisdom of a mud kitchen.

title: Who pays for the warming?
news: The editorial notes that countries that contributed least to emissions, as the Nepal floods show, face the steepest costs.
link: Climate justice asks those who caused the problem to pay for its harms: finance for clean energy and a funded Loss and Damage Fund are moral obligations, not charity.
question: "Climate change is as much an ethical problem as a scientific one." Discuss with reference to loss and damage.

title: Promises that are never audited
news: Ahead of COP31, only two countries had filed transparency reports by late October, and only about 5% of 203 voluntary climate initiatives since 2015 met their goals.
syllabus: Environmental ethics; Ethics in international relations; Climate justice
link: Pledges without reporting are promises without accountability. Fairness between nations requires the North to deliver promised finance, and fairness to future generations requires everyone to report honestly against what they promised.
question: "Climate commitments without transparency are a breach of trust with future generations." Discuss.

title: When supply chains become weapons
news: China dominates global critical mineral processing and has used it as leverage in trade tensions; India plans a scheme to build its own processing base.
syllabus: Ethical issues in international relations; Environmental ethics
link: Using control over resources the whole world needs to coerce others turns interdependence into a weapon, raising a question of fairness between nations. As India builds its own base, it also owes a duty to its mineral regions: self-reliance should not come at the cost of land, water and local communities.
question: Is it ethical for nations to use their control over critical resources as leverage in international relations? Discuss.

title: When the strong flout the rules
news: P4M, co-sponsored by India, pledges a fair, equitable and inclusive multilateralism as major powers reject or flout the rules.
syllabus: Ethical issues in international relations; Environmental ethics
link: A rules-based order protects the weak from the strong; when powerful states flout rules with impunity, justice between nations gives way to power. Fair institutions, public engagement and care for the planet are the ethical basis for a renewed multilateralism.
question: "Multilateralism is the ethics of international relations put into practice." Discuss.
